rows.question: By roughly how much does the IPCC project extreme daily precipitation to intensify for each 1°C of global warming?
What happens to the intensity and frequency of hot extremes with each additional 0.5°C of global warming, per AR6?
According to Chapter 11, what is the assessed link between human greenhouse-gas emissions and temperature extremes?

Given that the IPCC says the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation is very likely to collapse abruptly before 2100, how should coastal planners prepare?
Given that the IPCC says mean wind speeds are projected to decline everywhere in Asia including South Asia, is wind power still viable in India?

caveats: Thresholds and question wording were fixed before this run, from TypeSafe's documented starting points; the dev set steers development by protocol, so any later retune on these numbers makes them optimistic.
The dev set is IPCC-knowledge questions, not front-door questions with a place and a horizon; the 14 paraphrase probes are closer to front-door wording but were authored, not sampled from users.
Counts are small: 2 dev items should be refused inside the silent bucket, and 7 probes. A difference of one item is not evidence of a difference.
No prompt-injection probes were sent to Jev: TypeSafe's terms bar testing their systems, and the dev set has no labelled injection items.

Dev labels corrected after the first Jev run, each with its evidence in its notes in evals/gold_set.json: CID-06, CID-11. Jev's disagreement prompted the check, so the figures above carry a selection effect; adr/0002 says how the other cid-table labels were re-read.

extreme daily precipitation events are projected to intensify by about 7% for each 1°C of global warming
every additional 0.5°C of global warming causes clearly discernible increases in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes, including heatwaves

It is an established fact that human-induced greenhouse gas emissions have led to an increased frequency and/or intensity of some weather and climate extremes since pre-industrial time, in particular for temperature extremes
there is medium confidence of heat extremes increasing in frequency in many parts of India

In 2019, atmospheric CO2 concentrations were higher than at any time in at least 2 million years ( high confidence), and concentrations of CH4 and N2O were higher than at any time in at least 800,000 years (very high confidence).
Each 1000 GtCO2 of cumulative CO2 emissions is assessed to likely cause a 0.27°C to 0.63°C increase in global surface temperature with a best estimate of 0.45°C

changes in precipitation extremes (heavy precipitation) generally do not follow those in average precipitation, and can even move in the opposite direction (e.g., with average precipitation decreasing but extreme precipitation increasing)
negative surface wind speed trends (stilling) were found in the tropics and mid-latitudes of both hemispheres
reaching annual averages of 410 parts per million (ppm) for carbon dioxide (CO 2), 1866 parts per billion (ppb) for methane (CH 4), and 332 ppb for nitrous oxide (N 2O) in 2019.

The future occurrence of low-likelihood, high-impact events linked to climate extremes is generally associated with low confidence , but cannot be excluded, especially at global warming levels above 4°C.
A long-term warming trend in annual mean surface temperature has been observed across Asia during 1960–2015, and the warming accelerated after the 1970s ( high confidence)

the very likely range of equilibrium climate sensitivity is between 2°C (high confidence) and 5°C ( medium confidence). The AR6 assessed best estimate is 3°C with a likely range of 2.5°C to 4°C (high confidence), compared to 1.5°C to 4.5°C in AR5, which did not provide a best estimate

the intensification of heavy precipitation will follow the rate of increase in the maximum amount of moisture that the atmosphere can hold as it warms ( high confidence), of about 7% per 1°C of global warming
The frequency and intensity of hot extremes (including heatwaves) have increased, and those of cold extremes have decreased on the global scale since 1950 ( virtually certain)
precipitation will generally become more frequent and more intense with additional global warming

Monsoon precipitation is projected to increase in the mid- to long term at the global scale, particularly over South and South East Asia, East Asia and West Africa apart from the far west Sahel ( high confidence )
Concurrent heatwaves and droughts have become more frequent, and this trend will continue with higher global warming ( high confidence )

The frequency and intensity of heavy precipitation events have increased since the 1950s over most land area for which observational data are sufficient for trend analysis ( high confidence), and human-induced climate change is likely the main driver
Mountain and polar glaciers are committed to continue melting for decades or centuries ( very high confidence)
It is virtually certain that the Arctic will continue to warm more than global surface temperature, with high confidence above two times the rate of global warming.
Cities intensify human-induced warming locally, and further urbanization together with more frequent hot extremes will increase the severity of heatwaves ( very high confidence )
The frequency of hot temperature extreme events will very likely increase nonlinearly with increasing global warming, with larger percentage increases for rarer events
Median increase of more than 25% in the 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level (Li et al., 2021)
Significant increases in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes and significant decreases in the intensity and frequency of cold extremes (Zahid and Rasul, 2012
Extreme heat events are very likely to become more intense and/or more frequent in SAS, WCA, ARP , EAS, and SEA by the end of 21st century
There is medium confidence of future declining mean SWS in Asia, except in SAS and SEA, as global projections indicate a decreasing trend
